title: The quarrelling quails
hookLine: the quails lift the net together and fly off, until they start to bicker (Jataka 33)

cards: Any group that's pulled off something hard together, a band, a team, a family moving house, knows the moment it starts to go wrong. It's rarely the big challenge that breaks it. It's the small stuff.
Who left the dishes. Who didn't pull their weight. This Jataka is set in a forest where many thousands of quails live under one wise leader, and the leader, in this telling, is the Buddha-to-be.
A bird-catcher lived nearby. He'd imitate the quail call, throw his net over them when they gathered, and carry them off to sell. So the wise quail made a plan.

teach.h: HEADS THROUGH THE MESH, AND LIFT.
teach.b: When the net falls on us, the leader says, every one of you put your head through a hole in the mesh. Then all together, lift, and fly. Carry the net to a thorn bush, drop it there, and slip out from underneath.

teach.h: THE NET FLOATS OFF LIKE A SAIL.
teach.b: The next time the bird-catcher throws his net, thousands of little heads pop up through the mesh, and the whole net rises like a sail and floats off to a thorn bush.
He spends the evening untangling it from the thorns, empty-handed. Day after day. His wife starts asking questions.
Then one day, as the quails are landing to feed, one accidentally steps on another's head.
Who stepped on my head? I did, sorry, I didn't mean it. But the other one won't let it go, and the argument grows.

Oh, I suppose you think you're the one lifting the whole net by yourself? The wise quail sees it and knows: when quarreling starts, disaster isn't far behind. He leads the quails who'll follow him away to another place.
The bird-catcher bides his time. A few days later he throws his net again, over the ones who stayed, and they're still bickering. You lift it.
No, you lift it. I lifted it last time, your turn.
While they argue about who should lift, nobody lifts at all, and he gathers the net and carries them all away. The enemy isn't what beats them. The net was always there.
It only closed when they stopped lifting together.

how: The quail story is told in Buddhist communities as a lesson in harmony, and harmony in the sangha, the monastic community, is something Buddhist monastic rules work hard to protect.

o: a song sung at dawn to wake the village
living in harmony, getting along together
a bird call used to gather the flock

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: made the plan, then left the quarrel
what they said as the net closed

s: the bird-catcher finally invented a better net
the net was the same. the quails stopped lifting together.
the quarrel started over an accident
one quail stepped on another's head while landing.
the wise quail led his followers away
when quarreling starts, he said, disaster isn't far behind.

games.q: you're the wise quail. the flock has started bickering about who does the lifting. what do you do?
o: take the side of whoever's right.
lead the ones who'll listen somewhere else.
games.why: he leads his followers away. the ones who stay are still arguing when the net falls, and nobody lifts.

practice: Think of a group you belong to, a family, a team, a household, and any small squabble going on: who does what, whose turn it is. Picture everyone under the same net.
Now picture yourself, instead of arguing about who should lift, just lifting your end, with no score kept.

wordCard.voice: Sammodamana. Living in harmony: the quails who together lifted the bird-catcher's net and flew free, until they started bickering about who was lifting.

orig.note: Pali: living in harmony, rejoicing together. The story is the Sammodamana Jataka.

carryVoice: Your line: together we lift the net. Thousands of little heads, one rising sail. Eighty-eight days now.
